doc.title: Ralph LaLama interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 23, 2010

title: Teaching and playing in Italy and Europe; jazz as American art
summary: He teaches in Assisi with the Vanguard band and near Venice, and says audiences abroad respect jazz as America's original art form.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You’ve spent some time in Italy right?

Well I do some teaching over there and actually with the Vanguard band we go once a year to Assisi, where we play a couple of concerts and we also do clinics, you know? And at one time I did something for the Manhattan School of Music, about five years in a row, we went to a place close to Venice, it was called Tuscafarco, and we were there for two weeks, all teaching and playing too, playing too, concerts. The faculty played at night and then we taught all day for two weeks. I did that for about five years in a row. That was nice, yeah. And then other times, just go there, in spots. I went to Spain, did a couple of clinics there on my own, and I mean with the bands too. I go with the Vanguard band, we’ll do clinics individually and in sections sometimes.
Do the people over there — I don’t know if “respect” is the right word — do they think of jazz as more significant than here?

Yeah. Because this is our gift to them. This is the only original art form that America has to offer. Original art form. I mean rock & roll is not original, it’s not American. You know classical music is not original. I mean there’s a lot of American composers but they’re not original. I mean they might be original in their own music but I’m saying the idea of classical music is not American. The idea of jazz is American, it’s an original American art form. So this is our gift to Japan, our gift to Germany. And a lot of people try to copy it. So yeah I would say they respect it. Oh yeah. Definitely. Totally.
